questions.prompt: A Stripe API v1 POST executed with a key returns 500. What does a later retry with that same key normally return?

choices.text: A different key automatically generated by the server.
The saved first response, including the 500.
A guaranteed fresh execution until it returns 200.
A new resource because failures never save results.

questions.explanation: API v1 saves the first executed result, including errors. Its semantics must not be confused with API v2 retry behavior.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 saves the first status and body after endpoint execution begins and returns that saved result for retries with the same key, including 500 responses.

questions.prompt: A Stripe API v1 key is reused with different request parameters. What should the client expect?

choices.text: An error identifying inconsistent reuse.
A second operation accepted under the same saved identity.
A merged request containing both old and new parameters.
A valid retry merely because the key string is unchanged.

questions.explanation: The idempotency layer compares parameters to prevent misuse. Reusing one key for a different operation is not a valid retry.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 compares retry parameters, permits pruning after at least 24 hours, and does not save pre-execution validation failures.

questions.prompt: An order commit succeeds, then the process crashes before publishing its event. Which inconsistency is possible?

choices.text: The database automatically rolls back because publishing was skipped.
Every subscriber infers the event directly from the client timeout.
A normal broker publish and database commit are automatically one transaction.
The order exists but downstream services never hear the event.

questions.explanation: The independent operations leave a dual-write gap. A database commit does not imply broker publication or automatic rollback.

sources.title: Transactional outbox pattern
sources.claim: Separate database commit and event publication can fail independently, producing missing or invalid notifications.

questions.prompt: How does an outbox table close the database-to-message dual-write gap?

choices.text: Store the event only in application memory until the next request.
Write the event in a separate transaction after deleting the state.
Commit business state and the event record in one transaction.
Publish first and assume the database cannot fail afterward.

questions.explanation: A single database transaction makes the state and event record consistent. A relay can publish committed rows afterward; independent writes preserve the gap.

sources.title: Transactional outbox pattern
sources.claim: Business data and outbox events are written in one transaction, then a relay publishes committed rows; consumers still need idempotent processing.

questions.prompt: A client times out after sending a create request and cannot tell if it succeeded. Which retry is appropriate?

choices.text: Send the original request without any retry identity.
Repeat the request with its original key and parameters.
Generate a fresh key and assume the first operation failed.
Change the amount while retaining the original saved key.

questions.explanation: The same key and parameters let the server recognize the uncertain retry. Changing the operation or key can duplicate or conflict with it.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 idempotency keys identify retries of the same operation.

questions.prompt: A Stripe API v1 request fails parameter validation before execution begins. What distinguishes this from an executed 500 result?

choices.text: There is no saved idempotent result from that failed validation.
The invalid request is saved as a permanently successful operation.
All future keys become invalid until the account is recreated.
The server must replay the same validation error forever.

questions.explanation: The save boundary is endpoint execution. Pre-execution validation failures can be retried without a saved result; an executed result can be replayed.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 does not save results before execution begins, including parameter-validation failures.

questions.prompt: Which statements apply to Stripe API v1 idempotent requests? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Retry the same operation with the same idempotency key.
Saved executed results can include a 500 response.
Use a new key for every retry of an uncertain operation.
The key guarantees a successful result rather than a replayed failure.
API v1 and API v2 necessarily have identical error replay behavior.

questions.explanation: A is correct: The key identifies retries of one operation. B is correct: API v1 replays the saved status and body. C is incorrect: A new key can create a second operation. D is incorrect: Idempotency prevents duplication, not all failures. E is incorrect: The documentation distinguishes their retry semantics.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 saves the first status and body after endpoint execution begins and returns that saved result for retries with the same key, including 500 responses.

questions.prompt: Which Stripe API v1 key-lifecycle statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A pruned key can create a new request if reused later.
Pre-execution validation failure does not save an idempotent result.
Every key is retained permanently without lifecycle limits.
Use personal sensitive information as the recommended key format.
A retry’s parameters must match the original operation.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Pruning removes the original saved identity. B is correct: Endpoint execution has not begun. C is incorrect: Keys can be removed after they are at least 24 hours old. D is incorrect: The guide advises sufficiently random keys without sensitive data. E is correct: Mismatches are rejected.

sources.title: Stripe idempotent requests
sources.claim: Stripe API v1 compares retry parameters, permits pruning after at least 24 hours, and does not save pre-execution validation failures.

questions.prompt: Which failures motivate a transactional outbox? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume two sequential writes are atomic because they share a function.
Publish tentative changes and ignore later rollback.
Treat a successful database write as proof of successful broker delivery.
Database success followed by failed event publication.
Event publication followed by database rollback.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: A function boundary is not a distributed transaction. B is incorrect: Events should not describe rolled-back state. C is incorrect: The second operation can fail independently. D is correct: Downstream services can miss a committed change. E is correct: Consumers can act on state that never committed.

sources.title: Transactional outbox pattern
sources.claim: Separate database commit and event publication can fail independently, producing missing or invalid notifications.

questions.prompt: Which outbox design statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume the outbox alone guarantees exactly-once external side effects.
An outbox removes every consistency issue across all downstream databases.
Write business state and its outbox event in the same transaction.
Publish only rows from committed transactions.
Design consumers to tolerate duplicate event delivery.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Duplicate publication still requires consumer safeguards. B is incorrect: Cross-service transactions need additional coordination. C is correct: They commit or roll back together. D is correct: Rolled-back changes must not generate notifications. E is correct: A relay or broker can send an event more than once.

sources.title: Transactional outbox pattern
sources.claim: Business data and outbox events are written in one transaction, then a relay publishes committed rows; consumers still need idempotent processing.
